title: Winning by the Rules: Optimizing Weapons Reviews in the Age of Technological Innovation
gist: Nathan Wood and Jesse Hamilton argue that cutting red tape or curtailing weapons reviews cannot fix the mismatch between fast-iterating ML weapons and slow law-of-war/Directive 3000.09 reviews; instead the US and NATO should embed voluntary legal and operational military advisers in defense firms so review becomes continuous delta-based assessment, a structure that also hedges against oversight swings across administrations.

themes.theme: Review speed mismatch for ML systems

insights.claim: For AI/ML-enabled weapons, the test, evaluation, verification and validation required by review can take longer than a provider needs to develop the next model iteration.
insights.speaker: Nathan Wood and Jesse Hamilton
insights.so_what: Defense AI vendors face structural fielding delays regardless of procurement reform.
insights.quote: the test, evaluation, verification, and validation that review requires can take longer than a provider needs to develop the next iteration

insights.claim: For models with millions or billions of weights, small data or training changes can shift behavior significantly, so a review starting only at deployment-readiness both lags technology and forces costly rework of every iteration built on a defect.
insights.speaker: Nathan Wood and Jesse Hamilton
insights.so_what: End-of-pipe review creates compounding rework risk for defense AI programs.
insights.quote: it leaves procurement authorities far behind the technological curve, and any defect it uncovers forces costly rework of every iteration already built on top of it

insights.claim: Ukraine has shown militaries can adapt platforms, software, EW and doctrine on timescales of days, which is generally not the case in the US and NATO.
insights.speaker: Nathan Wood and Jesse Hamilton
insights.so_what: Highlights the adaptation gap driving pressure for acquisition reform.

insights.claim: Bureaucratic reform cannot eliminate the fundamental challenges ML systems pose for rapid testing and verification, and many seemingly unnecessary rules are residue of past deadly mishaps.
insights.speaker: Nathan Wood and Jesse Hamilton
insights.so_what: Deregulatory acquisition reform may deliver less speed than expected for AI weapons.
insights.quote: many seemingly unnecessary rules are the residue of past, even deadly mishaps

insights.claim: The US is not party to Additional Protocol I but has conducted law of war weapons reviews as policy since 1974, now required by DoD Directive 5000.01, with Directive 3000.09 adding senior-level review for autonomous systems.
insights.speaker: Nathan Wood and Jesse Hamilton
insights.so_what: Review requirements are policy-based and thus changeable by administration, a regulatory risk for autonomy programs.

insights.claim: Curtailing evaluation risks filling arsenals with systems that are technically capable but cannot be safely or effectively deployed, because field manuals and training depend on documented system limits.
insights.speaker: Nathan Wood and Jesse Hamilton
insights.so_what: Speed-first acquisition could produce unusable inventory.
insights.quote: Curtailing evaluation risks filling arsenals with systems that are technically capable yet cannot be safely or effectively deployed.

insights.claim: Militaries should embed legal and operational advisers inside defense firms, on a voluntary company-discretion basis, to make review a continuous process alongside development rather than a discrete end hurdle.
insights.speaker: Nathan Wood and Jesse Hamilton
insights.so_what: Could reshape defense-tech compliance workflows and favor firms that opt into openness.
insights.quote: review becomes a continuous process running alongside development
insights.locator: Rather than relying on red-tape cuts

insights.claim: Embedded documentation lets reviewers assess deltas from already-examined baselines rather than starting from scratch, focusing scarce T&E resources on what is new.
insights.speaker: Nathan Wood and Jesse Hamilton
insights.so_what: Delta-based review could materially shorten AI weapons fielding timelines.
insights.quote: reviewing a deployment candidate becomes assessing deltas from already-examined baselines rather than starting from scratch

insights.claim: Existing Defense Contract Management Agency resident personnel oversee cost, schedule and spec conformance, not the legal and operational character of systems, so they do not solve this problem.
insights.speaker: Nathan Wood and Jesse Hamilton
insights.so_what: Identifies a gap in existing oversight institutions.
insights.locator: This may sound like already existing

insights.claim: Legal advisers can prevent firms from investing in unfieldable systems, for example by flagging training data of unclear provenance or possibly compromised inputs.
insights.speaker: Nathan Wood and Jesse Hamilton
insights.so_what: Data provenance is a latent fielding risk for defense AI firms.
insights.quote: accepting data of unclear provenance or possibly compromised inputs, sparing firms further investment in unfieldable systems
insights.locator: Our proposal calls for two kinds

insights.claim: Engineer-in-unit cells that speed combat iteration create larger documentation debt owed to reviewers, which embedded military advisers would pay down, so the two approaches are complements.
insights.speaker: Nathan Wood and Jesse Hamilton
insights.so_what: Faster battlefield iteration increases compliance burden unless documentation scales too.
insights.quote: The faster engineer-in-unit cells spin the develop-adapt loop, the larger the documentation debt owed to the reviewing body.

insights.claim: Voluntary embeds create competitive pressure because guarded firms yield thinner documentation and therefore slower review.
insights.speaker: Nathan Wood and Jesse Hamilton
insights.so_what: Openness becomes a competitive advantage in defense-tech procurement.
insights.quote: guarded firms yield thinner documentation and, consequently, slower review

insights.claim: Embeds risk capture under long exclusive tenure and raise concerns about the military picking winners, mitigated by audits, staggered tenures, non-competes, and prioritizing firms where research most outpaces review.
insights.speaker: Nathan Wood and Jesse Hamilton
insights.so_what: Implementation risks that could limit or bias adoption.
insights.quote: Long, exclusive tenure is a recipe for capture

insights.claim: Because oversight swings like a pendulum between administrations, the biggest schedule risk to a multi-administration weapons program may be tomorrow's review standards, which a continuous military-authored record hedges against.
insights.speaker: Nathan Wood and Jesse Hamilton
insights.so_what: Regulatory reversal risk is a key, under-appreciated risk for long-dated autonomy programs.
insights.quote: the greatest schedule risk may not be today’s review standards but tomorrow’s
insights.locator: This architecture has a further advantage

insights.claim: Most NATO members carry an Article 36 obligation under Additional Protocol I that the US does not, but implementation is uneven, so a common documentation standard would help allies meet existing obligations.
insights.speaker: Nathan Wood and Jesse Hamilton
insights.so_what: A shared standard could ease cross-allied defense-tech exports and procurement.
insights.locator: This calls for a review process
